column2: Wunsch resigns at once; returns at one in the morning to collect his belongings and leaves before dawn, as agreed with the Board; Molly Gregory hears him carrying his books
With Dreier away on vacation at Lake George, Molly Gregory gathers the whole community; Herbert Miller announces the truth about Wunsch's arrest

1945 summer institutes: art — Gropius, Lyonel Feininger, Ossip Zadkine, Alvin Lustig, Mary Callery, Robert Motherwell; music — Roland Hayes, Carol Brice, Erwin Bodky, Hugo Kauder, Alfred Einstein; complaint: too many events
Carol Brice, who came with her mother and her baby, stays four weeks and gives several concerts
Carol Brice's last concert; the same day Roland Hayes arrives (with his wife and daughter); at the party at the Lowinskys', Hayes sings his unpublished arrangements of spirituals
Wunsch returns to Louisiana, ill for several months (“a bad jaw infection”), then goes to California, where he disappears (a postal clerk, according to rumor)

The Wallens visit Black Mountain; two “vocal” faculty members (Albers suspected) delay the appointment over a rumor (letter from Gordon Allport, July 19, 1945) of a discharge for “nervous instability,” denied by the army

Roland Hayes's public concert (accompanist Reginald Boardman, from New Hampshire): the largest crowd in the college's history, ~400 people, including 300 outside guests and 30 to 40 Black people; unsegregated seating (“Wherever you please”); no incidents
Photo 14: John Wallen and his son Kurt in front of the Wallens' apartment, 1945-46

Sylvesta (“Vesta”) Martin, who came to the Music Institute, stays on as the first full-time Black student; Dr. Percy H. Baker, “visiting lecturer” in biology for the fall term 1945 (700 dollars, Rosenwald Fund)

The college chorus (with Vesta Martin) prepares Schütz's St. Matthew Passion for a white Methodist church in Black Mountain; veto by the church board; the chorus sings at the Black church (conflicting accounts of the attendance)

Start of the 1945 year: nine new faculty members (eight young Americans with children), one-year appointments; 60 students (25% men); GI Bill approval (music, English, social sciences, mathematics, chemistry on condition)

Arrivals: John L. Wallen (age 27, psychology, Harvard doctorate), Albert William “Bill” Levi (philosophy), and Mary Caroline Richards (literature and writing), from Chicago; Theodore Rondthaler (finances, Latin); Max Dehn (mathematics, Plato, ethics; Sunday hikes)
The Board of Fellows adopts a new appointment policy: a first trial year, then renewals of one, two, three, and five years
Dreier on leave in Cambridge for nearly all of 1945-46, elected rector in absentia after Wunsch's departure; periodic visits to the college

Wallen's courses: “Introduction to psychology” (no textbook, T.A.T. at the start of the course) and a seminar on the teacher-student relationship (Cantor, The Dynamics of Learning; Rank, Fromm, Rogers, Horney); a session on Oedipus Rex
Faculty study group on “the aims of education at BMC”: a single session, the second never takes place

Wallen's students: two afternoons a week accompanying a young patient from a nearby psychiatric hospital, Southern Negro Youth Congress, petitions, voter registration; the question of the picket line at the Lucky Strike plant
Wallen on the admissions committee: choice of an “imaginative and erratic” student over a good one; the student later has difficulties
After the war, no professional farmer: Molly Gregory plows, harrows, brings in the harvest, runs the dairy with students
Expenses: food 23,595 dollars in 1945-46, 36,279 in 1946-47; living costs 42,110 then 64,281 dollars

Evening of students at the Wallens': the idea of reforming the work program (a 12,000-dollar deficit); questionnaire; petition for a community meeting signed by 34 students and 11 faculty members (including Jalowetz and Lowinsky)

Faculty meeting: Wallen presents his method (suggestion box 36 hours ahead, seven groups of twelve, three questions of twenty minutes, coffee and cake, a general list); objections (Albers), then a “vote of confidence”

Death of Heinrich Jalowetz from a heart attack after a recital of Beethoven sonatas, sitting on the porch; Johanna Jalowetz and the Lockwoods keep vigil listening to the St. Matthew Passion, Brahms's Clarinet Quintet, Mozart, Bach's Cello Suites
Second term 1945-46: the Black composer Mark Fax succeeds Baker; no incidents during the year despite the visitors and the concerts by Vesta Martin and Mark Fax

Arthur Penn (age 24, formerly of the Neighborhood Playhouse in Philadelphia, army theater), on the strength of his brother Irving Penn's stories about the Bauhaus, makes a two-week visit and then enrolls as a student

“Report of Faculty Committee” (Wallen, Levi, Rondthaler): an eight-member Community Council (three faculty, three students, one representative of the wives and staff, one of the community), a joint disciplinary committee with the power of expulsion, majority vote in the faculty when there is no consensus, two-thirds referendum; adopted over a series of community and faculty meetings
Thanks to the GI Bill, 75 students in spring 1946 in facilities planned for 60 at most
Albers speaks to a student of Wallen's “bid for power” and urges his own advisees to support his candidates in the Community Council elections

Photo 16: 1946 summer institute — Leo Amino, Jacob Lawrence, Leo Lionni, Ted and Bobbie Dreier, Beaumont Newhall, Gwendolyn Lawrence, Ise Gropius, Varda, Nan Newhall, Walter Gropius, Molly Gregory, Josef and Anni Albers
Wallen elected chairman of the new Community Council

Summer 1946: Music Institute suspended (Fritz Cohen's departure); Art Institute: Jean Varda, Leo Amino, Jacob Lawrence, Concetta Scaravaglione, Balcomb Greene, Will Burtin, Leo Lionni, Beaumont Newhall, briefly Gropius

Arrival of Karl Niebyl (Marxist economist born in Prague, his dissertation burned by the Nazis, formerly at Tulane, Carleton, Wisconsin) with three disciples; encourages involvement in the Southern Negro Youth Congress
Affair of the “47” telegram opened by mistake (47 votes the day before at a community meeting): a student is interrogated; the telegram came from a Republican friend

Wallen study group (15 to 20 people, mostly students) on small communities; weekends of shared work (a dam on the stream feeding Lake Eden); scouting for sites (Maine, Utah, Oregon); the Rondthalers, Liz Gellhorn, and Dave Resnik drop out
1946-47: 90 students, more than 50% men (end of the wartime “girls' school” character); applicants turned away

Rondthaler obtains three army-surplus buildings: student studies, classrooms and storage, and the first well-lit library (for Nell Rice, librarian); government donations after that (printing press, furniture, typewriters, dishwasher, meat grinder, a hundred swivel chairs, a sewer snake, a trouser press)
Two Quaker couples, the Clifford Moles and the Raymond Trayers, take over the farm; students and faculty enlarge the farm

No deficit in 1946-47, and even a reserve of 618.41 dollars; 1947-48: projected income 115,239, expenses 119,402 dollars; Rondthaler underspends for seven months; the fiscal year ends in surplus thanks to gifts and the summer institutes
Charlotte (“Bimbus”) Schlesinger hired in music; Johanna Jalowetz teaches singing and bookbinding

Josef and Anni Albers on a year's leave in Mexico; Ilya Bolotowsky (noticed at his retrospective at J. B. Neumann's New Art Circle) replaces them; Trude Guermonprez, the Jalowetzes' elder daughter, teaches weaving in place of Anni Albers (1947), then stays on as an assistant the following year
Ilya Bolotowsky teaches painting (permissive, all styles), stays until spring 1948; Studebaker runs into South Carolina to buy liquor (a dry county)
Community meeting against TAC's dormitory (“a barracks or a beach house”); preference for small dormitories of 10 to 14 people; plans drawn up by students; the Board pays TAC but abandons the project
Student resolution: admit as many Black students as possible, men included; fund-raising during the Christmas vacation; the faculty unanimously accepts Black men
Winter term 1947: five Black students, including two male veterans; the “experimental” phase declared over, public statement: “admission will be open to all students of all races”
Survey of former students (admission to graduate school); summary in the BMC Bulletin vol. 6 no. 1 (January 1948)
Edward Lowinsky leaves for Italy on a Guggenheim fellowship, then for Queens College

A Fellowship of Reconciliation group, including Bayard Rustin, spends a night at the college during its trip through the South to test segregation (Journey of Reconciliation); BMC “the only known haven” in the region for interracial groups
“Re: Wallen Proposal” by Mary Caroline Richards (five pages); permissive response from the Board; opposition from the Alberses; Wallen holds to his resignation
Molly Gregory resigns as secretary of the corporation and declines reelection to the Board; Albers: she has “sold him down the river”
Departure of the Wallens and the “Oregon crowd”
Frank Rice, son of John Andrew Rice, joins the faculty
Summer 1947: institutes effectively suspended (Albers away, music depleted); Beaumont Newhall and Carol Brice return; Erich Kahler's lectures on “World Government” and “The Crisis of the Individual”
Kenneth Noland takes a single term with Albers, then works with Ilya Bolotowsky (Albers's replacement during a year of leave in the late 1940s)
Only one of the five Black students returns in fall 1947 (she stays several years); no new recruitment

Penn's theater class twice a week: 20 to 30 participants, including Levi, M. C. Richards, and Wallen; An Actor Prepares, improvisations; a stage built at the end of the dining hall (Penn rewires the old switchboard)
Productions by Penn's class: an evening of burlesque skits, then Sartre's Huis clos (No Exit), Saroyan's Hello Out There, Edna St. Vincent Millay's Aria da Capo

The Board asks for plays to be performed again for “important” visitors; Wallen's “Group Process” class plays out the conflict (vote of 11 to 1); solution: a presentation of the work (improvisations, set changes with the curtain open, testimonies, one scene played again)

Seven or eight students (Paul Williams, Al Lanier, Si Sillman) spend about a year building the “Minimum House” (a little over 1,000 dollars, paid by Paul Williams's mother); Jalowetz's tombstone built into the back wall by mistake

Fall 1947 program: Levi (“Logic,” “The Individual in Society”), M. C. Richards (poetry, fiction), Rondthaler (Latin, “History of the English Language”), Frank Rice (German, arrived in summer 1947), Wallen (“Group Process”), Max Dehn (“Problems of Philosophy”); Tasker Howard Jr., a former student back from the NLRB (economics); Natasha Goldowski (physics, chemistry; formerly of the Manhattan Project) and her mother, “Madame” (French, Russian)

The Levis move into the Dreiers' apartment at “Roadside” (half of a house shared with the Alberses): disorder in the shared living room, a quarrel over the furnace; Levi and Albers stop speaking to each other
Charles Bloomstein, a certified public accountant, joins the staff (the college's books, the accounts of the farm, the store, the workshops)
The Alberses return from Mexico, “a few months” before the visit of Cage and Cunningham
The Alberses return from Mexico “in the early spring of 1948”; Albers disapproves of courses taught by students and of the weight given to the social sciences

Bolotowsky's students against Albers (the “illusionism” of the material exercises); according to Bolotowsky, Albers has the exhibition room floor varnished too heavily for it to dry before the opening

The “Anonymous Blotch” affair: a canvas covered with the leftover paint from the palettes of Bolotowsky's students (Hank and John Bergman, Joe Fiore, Jerrold Levy, Stan Hebel, Kenneth Noland) in Hebel's room, hung in the dining hall; Bolotowsky defends it as “post-Dali”; Albers's anger

New payment on the first mortgage; a 10,000-dollar debt becomes the first lien (1,000 dollars a year over ten years); second mortgage of 16,500 dollars held by the Dreier family; loan of 9,500 dollars from Stephen Forbes
The Wallenites found the Oregon community (“an outgrowth of Black Mountain”); dissolved after three years; a five-day annual reunion at Thanksgiving

1948 summer session: 74 students (half of them new); guests: Willem and Elaine de Kooning, Richard and Louise Lippold (who arrived in a hearse), Buckminster Fuller (invited by Albers), Peter Grippe, Richard Lischer (woodworking), Winslow Ames (history of printmaking, July), Beaumont Newhall (3rd summer, History of Photography), Charles Burchard (architecture, August), Erwin Bodky (“Sonatas of Beethoven”), Edgar Kaufmann Jr. (industrial design), Isaac Rosenfeld (Tolstoy, writing), John Cage, Merce Cunningham; Josef Albers, Anni Albers, Trude Guermonprez

Buckminster Fuller's course in architecture and industrial engineering; four- to five-hour lectures with an intermission and tables of geometric figures; friendship between Fuller and de Kooning (errands in Asheville)
Merce Cunningham's only solo concert for the community, assisted by Louise Lippold (a former pupil) and Sara Hamill (a pupil); Cunningham's classes

Cage's Satie “Amateur Festival”: 25 half-hour concerts, three evenings a week after dinner, in the dining hall or at the piano in his cottage with the windows open; plus a concert of his own works; Albers insists on a ten-minute talk before each concert
Mary Caroline Richards translates Satie's Le Piège de Méduse at the Rondthalers' in Ocracoke and returns toward the end of the summer
The Levis go to the Rondthalers' in Ocracoke, before Europe
According to Bolotowsky, Levi asks him to stay on to “dump Albers”; he refuses; Bolotowsky leaves the college
Dreier serves temporarily as rector after Levi's resignation
At lunch, Levi proposes a kitchen “duel” as rector (cold schnitzels against crêpes Suzette); a food fight, “some thirty people got themselves pretty messed up”
Halfway through the festival, Cage gives a long talk against Beethoven (“Beethoven was in error”); Erwin Bodky responds with a concert of Beethoven's late quartets preceded by a talk
Fuller attempts to erect his first large geodesic dome (aluminum Venetian-blind strips, 15 m planned) in the rain: the “Supine Dome” does not rise
Open rehearsals of Le Piège de Méduse; Arthur Penn called in to direct; exercises to “make a damn fool of myself” with Fuller

Performance of Satie's Le Piège de Méduse (The Ruse of Medusa), translated by M. C. Richards: Buckminster Fuller (Baron Méduse), Elaine de Kooning, Merce Cunningham (the mechanical monkey, tail designed by Lippold), Isaac Rosenfeld, Alvin Charles Few (nephew of the cook Malrey Few); sets by Willem de Kooning; Cage at the piano; directed by Arthur Penn; the Levis come back for the occasion
The Levis leave for their year in Europe

Enrollment down from 90 to 50 students in fall 1948; resignations posted on the bulletin board; faculty: Anni and Josef Albers, Erwin Bodky, Trude Guermonprez, Johanna Jalowetz, Charlotte Schlesinger, Natasha Goldowski, Anna Goldowski, Frank Rice
Edward Dahlberg arrives to replace M. C. Richards (literature, writing); individual conferences (boys in his office, girls on walks in the woods)
Robert Rauschenberg's first stay, with Susan Weil; Albers finds him frivolous (“had nothing to teach him”)
Olson's first class at Black Mountain; a student judges him “basically a charlatan” (letter from Mel Mitchell Kelly to “Andy,” November 20, 1949)
Natasha Goldowski's noncredit seminar on cybernetics from the proofs of Norbert Wiener's first book; Olson: it lacked a poet

Charles Olson, visiting teacher: monthly stays (often a week); “Writing” and “Reading” seminars, evening lectures (non-Homeric myth, Melville), poetry readings, tarot; a danced and mimed production of García Lorca's Llanto por Ignacio Sánchez Mejías
Albers and Dreier on a tour of the North to solicit gifts; Stephen Forbes refuses (“leaned slightly toward the Levi position”)

N. O. Pittenger's first visit at the end of January, at the height of the crisis; he refuses to commit himself until the annuity question (the Albers–Jalowetz–Straus pension, bonds in Albers's name) is cleared up
Professor Cole, a longtime auditor, comes to establish the legality of the pension plan; 80% of the funds protected; Pittenger accepts an advisory role; final resignations
Josef and Anni Albers, Trude Guermonprez, and Charlotte Schlesinger leave after their classes end; Nell Rice is the only one left of the 1933 group
Just before the summer session, visits by Langston Hughes and by Bortai Bunting, daughter of Basil Bunting

1949 summer session directed by Fuller (more than 50 students): John Walley and Emerson Woelffer (Institute of Design, drawing, painting, sculpture), Diana Woelffer and Jane Walley (ceramics, jewelry, photography), nine engineer-designers from the Institute of Design; Marli Ehrman (weaving), Betty and Pete Jennerjahn (dance, printing), Nataraj Vashi and Pia-Veena (Hindu dance and philosophy), James Albert Pait, Nathan Rosen, John Scholtz (symposiums on infinity); Erwin Bodky (music)
Fuller's dome (a 4.3 m hemisphere of aircraft aluminum tubing and Vinylite, built at the Institute of Design) stands; tests by the engineers; it sags in September
Fuller's big party for the community: a student reads aloud one of his two-hundred-page poems, read to the end
Three-day Bach festival directed by Erwin Bodky (who leaves the faculty in the fall)
The Rondthalers come back for a few weeks; appeal for funds to alumni; Forbes maintains the mortgage and releases the gravel land; the Board suspends the Alberses' monthly annuities for the summer

Charles Olson's evening “Wagadu, after Frobenius”: poetry, mime, music, color, dance (“jointure of speech-sound-motion”); his plan to bring his Washington troupe (Odyssey) turned down for lack of funds
The faculty gives Pittenger “all administrative prerogatives”: he becomes rector pending a permanent appointment
